title: The Terracotta Army was painted; dug up, its lacquer curls in about 15 seconds

cover.alt: Rows of life-sized terracotta soldiers standing in the long earthen corridors of Pit 1 near Xi’an, seen from above under the museum hall roof.

body: The more than **8,000 life-sized soldiers** buried near the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China’s first emperor, were once brightly coloured with pigments such as cinnabar red, azurite blue and Han purple laid over a lacquer base. Exposed to Xi’an’s dry air, that lacquer starts to curl within about 15 seconds and can flake off in about four minutes, which is why most figures look bare today and why much of the army is deliberately left in the ground. Farmers digging a well found the first fragments on 29 March 1974. No two faces are exactly alike: craftsmen individualised about ten basic face types by hand.

slides.alt: A museum display of the mineral pigments used on the terracotta warriors, in small heaps of red, blue, purple, green and white.
slides.caption: Pigments found on the warriors, buried around 210–209 BC near the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China’s first emperor. Their colours survived underground for some 2,200 years.

slides.question: How many soldiers are estimated to stand in the three pits?
slides.explanation: More than 8,000 soldiers, with 130 chariots, 520 chariot horses and 150 cavalry horses, by 2007 estimates. Most of them are still in the ground.

slides.heading: The army by the numbers (2007 estimates)
slides.note: Estimates; most of the army remains unexcavated in its three pits.

steps.label: A figure is dug out of damp soil
Dry air hits the lacquer base
The lacquer curls in about 15 seconds
Paint flakes off within four minutes

slides.heading: Ten faces, thousands of men
slides.text: Scholars have identified ten basic facial forms, which the craftsmen then individualised by hand, so that no two figures share exactly the same features. The soldiers stand about 1.75 to 2 m tall, officers taller still. Pit 1 alone, about 230 m long and 62 m wide, holds more than 3,000 of them.

slides.question: Who found the Terracotta Army in 1974?
options: A flood washing out a bank
slides.explanation: On 29 March 1974 farmers digging a well about 1.5 km east of the tomb mound struck the first fragments. The emperor’s tomb itself remains unopened.

left.label: The claim
left.text: Reports said Qin armourers coated bronze weapons in chromium to stop rust, two thousand years ahead of modern plating.

right.label: The finding
right.text: A 2019 study found the chromium was merely contamination from nearby lacquer. The slightly alkaline, fine-grained soil most likely preserved the bronze.
